newsitem.title: UK: Rash of UK data tip odds towards rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Rash of UK data tip odds towards rate rise.

text.p: A raft of economic data showing Britain's manufacturers perking up while consumer demand remains robust has shortened the odds of an interest rate rise this week, analysts said on Wednesday.
"The case for higher rates is pretty compelling and I think we will see a quarter-point tightening this week," said Adam Cole, UK economist at HSBC James Capel.
He said Monday's data showed Britain's sluggish manufacturers being helped out by the strength of domestic demand, which was offsetting export weakness.
Britain's purchasing managers index rose to a two-year high of 54.6 in May and showed the manufacturing sector expanded for the 12th month in a row.
"Buoyant domestic demand from consumers continued to boost order books," the Chartered Institute of Purchasing Supply said.

"Despite a further fall in the rate of growth of export orders, attributed to the sustained strength of the pound, UK manufacturers experienced the fastest growth of total orders since last November."

That will give serious food for thought for Britain's new-style monetary policy committee which meets for the first time on Thursday and Friday. Manufacturing has long been the laggard part of a generally buoyant UK economy.

"Despite the apparent lack of price pressures, the report is consistent with a continued expansion in the manufacturing sector," said Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Plc. "The odds remain just about in favour of a monetary tightening this week."
Four members from the Bank of England will sit down to discuss rates this week. A second deputy governor is yet to be elected.
And at some point, maybe before this week's meeting, Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown will nominate four non-Bank members to the committee.
If Brown's quartet are not chosen by Thursday, economists said there could be political problems for the Bank members, led by Governor Eddie George, tightening policy without any dissenting voices.

But Cole said, given the Bank's remit to meet a 2.5 percent underlying inflation target and its view, voiced loud and clear in its last inflation report, that the target will not be hit in two years' time, it will be hard for the four not to raise rates even if the non-Bank representation is missing.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown raised base rates by a quarter-point to 6.25 percent last month, after just five days in office.
M0 money supply and consumer credit data, released at the same time as the PMI were a little more modest in their implications.

M0, the narrow money supply measure, grew only 6.1 percent in the year to May, well below economists' forecasts of a 6.5 percent increase. But they said that sat uneasily next to evidence of still-robust consumer spending.
The third chunk of Monday's data round showed net consumer credit rose by 691 million stg in April. Again, that looks low, but the year-on-year rate of increase is still hefty at 16.5 percent.
"The deceleration of M0 over recent months is at odds with buoyant consumer spending and therefore rather curious," Shaw said.

Few analysts thought the data signalled a slowdown in the trend of carefree consumer spending. Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at BankAmerica, said April's drop in credit was a surprise. "But it may just reflect caution ahead of the election and upcoming budget."

Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown will announce the date of his budget later on Monday. If he decides to hold it next week, the monetary committee may hold rates in order to judge the impact of any fiscal tightening measures Brown introduces, Cole said.
"The only wild card is the budget date. If that was going to be very near-term then they may hold off. But if it's early July, as most people expect, they will want to act early."

But Hawkins said Monday's welter of figures should not be seen as strong enough to prompt a rate rise this week. But he conceded that consumer credit would soon pick up again and the economy is doing well -- "with perhaps a better balance to growth than previously seemed likely."
